name: Digital Markets Act
evidence_rating: early and thin: Commission review is qualitative; three studies with causal designs on individual remedies (browsers, Amazon ranking, maps) and one small study on start-ups; headline benefits never measured
summary: The DMA has changed gatekeeper conduct (choice screens, steering, alternative app stores, consent, less self-preferencing on Amazon) and produced EUR 1.59bn of fines, but none of the six promised indicators is reported systematically and the EUR 13bn consumer-surplus estimate has not been assessed. Causal studies find large default effects for browsers (Firefox +91% on iOS), a one-third drop in Amazon's self-preferencing after designation, but no shift to rival map services; one small study finds lower start-up entry and investment. Theory (Madio, Manenti & Motta 2026) supports the DMA's equal-access design.

indicators.objective: Address market failures to ensure contestable and competitive digital markets for increased innovation and consumer choice
Enhance coherence and legal certainty to preserve the internal market
Enhance coherence and legal certainty / limit diverging national regulatory interventions
indicators.indicator: Number of regulatory interventions at the national level
indicators.evidence: Not reported in the 2026 review. The review records stakeholder concerns about fragmentation and parallel national enforcement and requests for guidance on Article 1(6), but gives no count.

indicators.objective: Enhance coherence and legal certainty / ensure coherent interpretation of obligations
indicators.indicator: Number of clarification requests per year
indicators.evidence: Not reported. The review describes regulatory dialogue and possible guidelines but gives no count of clarification requests.

indicators.objective: Address gatekeepers' unfair conduct / prevent self-preferencing
indicators.indicator: Number of compliance interventions by the Commission per gatekeeper per year
indicators.evidence: Activity reported, not as the indicator: non-compliance proceedings opened against Alphabet, Apple and Meta (March 2024) and Apple (June 2024); two specification decisions on Apple interoperability (March 2025); one investigation into Apple's choice obligations closed after changes. Seven gatekeepers designated. Independent evidence of conduct change: Amazon's search-rank advantage for its own products fell from about 30 to about 20 positions soon after designation (Waldfogel 2024).

indicators.objective: Address gatekeepers' unfair conduct / prevent self-preferencing
indicators.indicator: Number of sanction decisions per gatekeeper per year
indicators.evidence: Four fines in two years of application: Apple EUR 500m (anti-steering) and Meta EUR 200m (pay or consent), 23 April 2025; Alphabet EUR 460m (search self-preferencing) and EUR 430m (Google Play anti-steering), 23 July 2026. Total EUR 1.59bn. Apple's decision is under appeal.

indicators.objective: Contestable markets / prevent unfair access and data practices
indicators.indicator: Share of users multi-homing with different platforms or services
indicators.evidence: Not measured by the Commission (review says it will monitor switching). Independent evidence on one remedy: after Google removed the Maps link from EU search results, users searched for 'google maps' instead; no robust shift to rival map services (Pape & Rossi 2026).

indicators.objective: Contestable markets / prevent unfair access and data practices
indicators.indicator: Share of users switching between different platforms and services
indicators.evidence: Commission cites company figures only (Aloha +250% new users; Firefox daily users doubled on iOS in DE and FR). Independent causal estimate: Firefox usage +91% on iOS and +13% on Android vs counterfactual after the choice-screen mandate; Safari declined on iOS with gains mostly to Chrome (Akesson et al. 2026). Consent: >45% of users (up to 90%) refuse data combination under Art 5(2).

indicators.indicator: Consumer surplus +EUR 13bn per year (about +6% vs baseline)
indicators.evidence: Not assessed in the 2026 review, which says impacts are not yet fully observable.

indicators.indicator: Cross-border trade gain of EUR 92.8bn by 2025

indicators.objective: Growth and jobs (Digital Single Market-wide, not DMA-specific)
indicators.indicator: GDP +0.44-0.82% and 307-561 thousand FTEs from a more efficient Digital Single Market
indicators.evidence: Not assessed; the figure is borrowed from Digital Single Market estimates and is not attributable to the DMA alone.

indicators.indicator: Greater innovation potential among smaller businesses
indicators.evidence: Mixed. Commission review: new third-party app stores on iOS (Epic, Aptoide, AltStore PAL) and gains for alternative browsers. Yang (2025): DMA reduced start-up entry and investment in DMA-related industries (difference-in-differences, 1,034 records). Oxera (2021, Amazon-funded experiment): such rules likely reduce innovation.

literature.citation: European Commission (2020), Impact Assessment Report accompanying the DMA proposal, SWD(2020) 363; Executive summary SWD(2020) 364
literature.headline: Consumer surplus +EUR 13bn/yr; compliance costs for gatekeepers not quantified; SMEs expected to benefit
literature.title: Impact Assessment Report accompanying the DMA proposal
literature.summary_plain: The Commission forecast that the DMA would raise consumer surplus by about EUR 13 billion a year, but did not estimate compliance costs for gatekeepers.

literature.citation: European Commission (2026), Staff Working Document accompanying the Report on the Review of the DMA, SWD(2026) 123, 28 April 2026
literature.method: qualitative review using compliance data, compliance reports and consultation
literature.outcomes: conduct change; user choice; entry of alternative providers
literature.headline: DMA 'has already created positive impacts' but 'has not yet achieved its full potential'; no legislative changes proposed; most impacts 'not yet fully observable'
literature.title: First review of the Digital Markets Act (staff working document)
literature.summary_plain: The Commission finds that the DMA has started to change how gatekeepers behave and to open their ecosystems, but says most effects cannot yet be measured and proposes no legislative changes.

literature.citation: European Commission (2025), press release: Commission finds Apple and Meta in breach of the DMA, 23 April 2025
literature.headline: Apple EUR 500m, Meta EUR 200m
literature.title: Commission finds Apple and Meta in breach of the Digital Markets Act
literature.summary_plain: First DMA fines: EUR 500 million for Apple (anti-steering in the App Store) and EUR 200 million for Meta (pay-or-consent).

literature.citation: European Commission (2026), press release: Commission fines Google EUR 890 million for breaches of the DMA, 23 July 2026
literature.headline: EUR 460m (search self-preferencing, Art 6(5)) and EUR 430m (Google Play anti-steering, Art 5(4))
literature.title: Commission fines Google EUR 890 million for breaches of the Digital Markets Act
literature.summary_plain: Google fined EUR 460 million for favouring its own services in search results and EUR 430 million for restricting app developers from steering users to cheaper offers outside Google Play.

literature.citation: Akesson, J., Amlani, K., Cepeda Suarez, R., Chissell, E., Hunt, S., Luca, M. & Petrie, G. (2026), Active Choice Interventions at Scale: Browser Defaults under the Digital Markets Act, NBER Working Paper 35112 (first issued April 2026 as "The Effect of Choice Screens on Mobile Browser Usage: Evidence from the EU Digital Markets Act")
literature.headline: From month 15, Firefox usage +91% on iOS and +13% on Android vs no-mandate counterfactual; Safari declined on iOS with gains concentrated in Chrome
literature.quality: strong design (difference-in-differences); not peer-reviewed; two authors are Mozilla employees and Mozilla provided the data (Firefox is an affected rival)
literature.authors: Akesson, Amlani, Cepeda Suarez, Chissell, Hunt, Luca, Petrie
literature.title: Active Choice Interventions at Scale: Browser Defaults under the Digital Markets Act
literature.summary_plain: Browser choice screens required by the DMA substantially increased use of rival browsers: Firefox usage rose 91% on iPhones and 13% on Android compared with what would otherwise have happened.
literature.interested_party: Two authors are Mozilla employees; Mozilla provided the data

literature.citation: Pape, L. & Rossi, M. (2026), research on the DMA's self-preferencing ban and Google Maps; summarised in ProMarket, 18 May 2026
literature.direction: null for rivals; small negative for user experience
literature.headline: Searches for 'google maps' +21% in EU vs non-EU; no robust gain for Bing Maps, Mappy, OpenStreetMap; total Google Maps desktop traffic unchanged; visit duration -5%, bounce rate +16%
literature.title: The DMA's Google Maps experiment
literature.summary_plain: When Google removed the direct link to Google Maps from EU search results, users simply searched for "google maps" instead; rival map services gained no meaningful traffic.

literature.citation: Yang, J. (2025), Unintended effects of Digital Market Act on new entry and investment, Digital Policy, Regulation and Governance, doi:10.1108/DPRG-03-2025-0080
literature.method: causal: difference-in-differences (1,034 start-up and investment records, 27 EU countries, 2020-2024)
literature.headline: DMA negatively affected new entry and investment in DMA-related industries
literature.quality: small sample; short post-period; abstract only
literature.title: Unintended effects of Digital Market Act on new entry and investment
literature.summary_plain: Using start-up and investment records from 27 EU countries, the study finds fewer new entrants and less investment in industries affected by the DMA.

literature.citation: Decarolis, F., Li, M. & Paternollo, F. A., Competition and Defaults in Online Search (working paper, Bocconi)
literature.method: causal: event studies of default interventions (EEA, Russia, Turkey)
literature.headline: Changes to default settings reduced Google's market share in all three cases; DMA-specific estimate not verified
literature.quality: abstract only; DMA-specific effect not confirmed
literature.title: Competition and Defaults in Online Search
literature.summary_plain: Across the EEA, Russia and Turkey, changes to default search settings reduced Google's market share; the DMA-specific effect has not been separately confirmed here.

literature.citation: Cabral, L., Haucap, J., Parker, G., Petropoulos, G., Valletti, T. & Van Alstyne, M. (2021), The EU Digital Markets Act: A Report from a Panel of Economic Experts, JRC
literature.headline: Supports intervention but warns legal uncertainty could chill innovation
literature.authors: Cabral, Haucap, Parker, Petropoulos, Valletti, Van Alstyne
literature.title: The EU Digital Markets Act: A Report from a Panel of Economic Experts
literature.summary_plain: Before adoption, a panel of economists supported intervention but warned that legal uncertainty could discourage innovation.

literature.citation: Oxera (2021), The Digital Markets Act and incentives to innovate: behavioural experiment (prepared for Amazon)
literature.headline: Interventions of this type likely to reduce total innovation in high digital-intensity industries
literature.title: The Digital Markets Act and incentives to innovate: behavioural experiment
literature.summary_plain: An experiment commissioned by Amazon suggests rules of this kind would reduce innovation in highly digital industries.
literature.interested_party: Commissioned by Amazon, a designated gatekeeper

literature.citation: CERRE (2025), Evaluating the DMA (DMA Implementation Forum), March 2025
literature.headline: Proposes effectiveness, efficiency and consistency dimensions and indicators for the Article 53 review; first year shows gains for users and complexity for firms and regulators
literature.title: Evaluating the DMA
literature.venue: CERRE DMA Implementation Forum report, March 2025
literature.summary_plain: Sets out how the DMA should be evaluated (effectiveness, efficiency, consistency) and which indicators to use; notes early gains for users and complexity for firms and regulators.

literature.citation: Madio, L., Manenti, F. M. & Motta, M. (2026), Platform Tying and its Effects, CEPR Discussion Paper 21771 (version of 21 July 2026)
literature.title: Platform Tying and its Effects
literature.headline: Tying a gatekeeper's own service can harm consumers who never use the gatekeeper, by shrinking rivals' seller base; demotion of rivals is always welfare-reducing in their simulations; a common-access rule of the DMA type removes the harm and remains profitable for the platform
literature.summary_plain: A theory paper showing why favouring a platform's own services can hurt even consumers who reach rivals directly, and that the DMA's equal-access approach removes this harm while remaining profitable for the platform. It does not measure the DMA's actual effects.
literature.quality: theory, not impact evidence; presented at "The Economics of the DMA" workshop (Brussels, 2025) and to DG Competition

literature.citation: Waldfogel, J. (2024), Amazon Self-preferencing in the Shadow of the Digital Markets Act, NBER Working Paper 32299
literature.title: Amazon Self-preferencing in the Shadow of the Digital Markets Act
literature.method: causal-leaning: before/after gatekeeper designation, compared with 142 other brands (8m+ search results, 22 Amazon domains)
literature.headline: Amazon's own products ranked about 30 positions better than comparable products; shortly after Amazon's designation as gatekeeper (Sept 2023) the advantage fell to about 20 positions, with no change for other brands; the change appeared in Europe and elsewhere
literature.summary_plain: Using over 8 million Amazon search results, the study finds Amazon's ranking advantage for its own products fell by about a third soon after the EU designated it a gatekeeper - and the change also showed up outside the EU.
literature.quality: strong data; not peer-reviewed; designation-timing comparison, no formal control market (change was global)

literature.citation: Farronato, C., Fradkin, A. & MacKay, A. (2023), Self-Preferencing at Amazon: Evidence from Search Rankings, AEA Papers and Proceedings 113: 239-243 (NBER w30894)
literature.title: Self-Preferencing at Amazon: Evidence from Search Rankings
literature.headline: Documents that Amazon-branded products rank higher in Amazon search than observably similar products (pre-DMA baseline for the self-preferencing ban)
literature.summary_plain: Pre-DMA evidence that Amazon ranks its own-brand products higher in search results than similar products - the kind of conduct the DMA's self-preferencing ban targets.

literature.citation: Motta, M. (2023), Self-preferencing and foreclosure in digital markets: Theories of harm for abuse cases, International Journal of Industrial Organization 90: 102974
literature.title: Self-preferencing and foreclosure in digital markets: Theories of harm for abuse cases
literature.headline: Sets out when self-preferencing by platforms can foreclose rivals and harm consumers; underpins the rationale for ex ante self-preferencing rules
literature.summary_plain: Explains the economic mechanisms by which a platform favouring its own products can exclude rivals - the theory behind the DMA's self-preferencing ban.
literature.verified: cited by Madio-Manenti-Motta; listed on author homepage

literature.citation: Motta, M. & Peitz, M. (2020), Intervention triggers and underlying theories of harm: expert advice for the Impact Assessment of a New Competition Tool, report for DG Competition
literature.title: Intervention triggers and underlying theories of harm
literature.venue: Expert report for DG Competition (cited in DMA impact assessment)
literature.headline: One of the expert reports the Commission commissioned for the New Competition Tool / DMA impact assessment, on structural competition problems and theories of harm
literature.summary_plain: An expert report commissioned by the Commission that fed into the impact assessment behind the DMA, setting out when intervention in digital markets is justified.
literature.quality: ex-ante expert opinion; cited in SWD(2020) 363 part 2
literature.verified: citation seen in impact assessment (search result); report text not read
